source_text: Sub nomine, inquiunt, gratiae ita fatum asserunt, ut dicant, quia nisi Deus invito et reluctanti homini inspiraverit boni et ipsius imperfecti cupiditatem, nec a malo declinare nec bonum possit arripere.
pass_a_gloss: Under the name of grace, they say, they so assert fate, that they say that unless God has breathed into an unwilling and resisting human being a desire of good — even of imperfect good — he can neither turn aside from evil nor seize good.

lemmas.lexica: LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: Under the name of grace they assert fate: they say that unless God breathes into an unwilling and resisting person a desire for good—even imperfect good—that person can neither turn away from evil nor take hold of good.

choices.why: In the suum cuique definition gratia is partiality, not saving grace.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian and fellow bishops (Collective letter to Thessalonica, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 2–4); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
